A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Wi-GATr and retain identifiable methods, experiments and appendices. The complete text, equations, tables and figures support comparison despite substantial rewriting and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original signal-prediction, receiver-localization and diffusion experiments on Wi3R and WiPTR, including additional analyses in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds evaluations on real DICHASUS measurements, a tokenizer ablation and additional timing analyses.

M1.justification: The geometric tokenizer, GATr backbone, predictive model and masked diffusion/inpainting procedure are retained. Section 5.4 explicitly applies the backbone to receiver arrays without modification; the additional pretraining comparison concerns experimental configuration.

E1.justification: v2 adds DICHASUS real-world measurements from a hallway with two receiver arrays, evaluating average received power and delay spread. This substantially extends v1's simulated-data coverage and adds an evaluated channel characteristic. Wi3R, WiPTR and their existing test scenarios remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds a transformer without the tokenizer to the Wi3R comparison in Figure 3, Learned Materials and Neural Materials to the real-data comparison in Figure 6, and Sionna with ground-truth or learned materials to Figure 8. The original predictive and diffusion comparators remain.

E3.justification: The new real-data evaluation uses array-averaged targets, two samples per transmitter location, varying training-set sizes, logarithmic power MAE and relative absolute delay-spread error. It also compares training from scratch with WiPTR pretraining. The reported splits and training budgets for the retained simulated-data experiments are unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses isolate the tokenizer's contribution on Wi3R, test simulation pretraining in the real-data small-sample regime, and measure inference scaling with token count. These substantially expand component attribution and scalability analysis beyond v1's retained symmetry, distribution-shift and geometry-generation checks.

E5.justification: Localization standard errors over 240 measurements and timing standard deviations are retained. New Figure 6 contains shaded bands, but neither their statistical meaning nor run or seed counts is specified. It is therefore unclear whether these introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds real-data power and delay-spread results, tokenizer-ablation results, Sionna comparisons and token-scaling measurements. Figure 3 also revises existing Wi3R curves: PLViT's full-data endpoint changes from approximately 5.7 to 4.8, and some Wi-GATr points change. The numerical entries in v1 Tables 2–3 are retained in v2 Tables 1–2.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds an explicit assumption that radiation patterns are shared within the transmitter and receiver populations and learned implicitly; v1's problem formulation did not state this restriction. The geometric-algebra definitions and diffusion mathematics are otherwise retained, without new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 adds claims of real-world superiority over hybrid methods and calibrated ray tracing, extends the highlighted tasks to delay-spread prediction, and explicitly claims the first fully learned surrogate operating on full 3D geometry. These broaden the scientific claims beyond v1's simulation-focused predictive and probabilistic contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning hybrid-model bias, pretraining, incomplete ray-tracing physics and quadratic inference scaling. Its limitations emphasize data-collection costs, implicit configuration and lack of drop-in equivalence to ray tracers, replacing v1's emphasis on restricted observables and idealized inverse problems. It also explicitly limits geometric-generalization conclusions from the single-hallway real-data study.

D1.justification: v2 documents the tokenizer-free baseline's coordinate representation, receiver-array handling, WiPTR pretraining and Sionna RT version 0.19's relevant physical-model restrictions. Existing architecture, optimizer, simulation and material details remain. Both versions still describe dataset publication as being prepared.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially repositions Wi-GATr against model-based, hybrid and fully learned simulation approaches, including a new full-3D novelty claim. New references include Hoydis et al. (2023), Euchner et al. (2021), Gloeckler et al. (2024), Lee and Molisch (2024), and Suk et al. (2024); several earlier background references are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, problem formulation and conclusion are extensively rewritten around learnable forward simulation. Receiver localization receives a separate subsection, while tokenizer details and much of the diffusion explanation and background move into reorganized appendices.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised to depict learning and gradients, Figure 3 gains an ablation curve and revised styling, and new Figure 6 presents two real-data plots. The timing figure expands into a two-panel comparison and scaling display. The tokenizer table moves from the main text to Appendix B, with broader layout and typography changes.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support was confined to simulated channels. v2 substantially strengthens practical validity through direct real-measurement evaluation against hybrid methods, while the tokenizer ablation improves attribution and the scaling analysis qualifies efficiency claims. The single-hallway scope and incomplete statistical and protocol details limit these gains, but the added evidence resolves an important gap in the original paper.
